explanations.explanation: Zedekiah is the king of Judah, and the LORD tells Jeremiah the prophet to go speak to him (Jeremiah 34:2). Jeremiah's message goes straight to the man wearing the crown. I'd be sweating just walking up to him with this news, and I only deliver cookies.

Jehoiakim was a king of Judah too, the son of Josiah (Jeremiah 36:1), so I see why he came to mind. But in this passage the LORD tells Jeremiah to go to Zedekiah king of Judah. Same kingdom, different king. I've mixed up two batches of dough before, and I didn't find out until the oven.

Ahab was a king of Israel (1 Kings 16:29), but he isn't the one in this passage. The LORD tells Jeremiah to speak to Zedekiah king of Judah (Jeremiah 34:2). Jerusalem is under attack, and Zedekiah is the king the message is for. Right title, wrong crown, friend. Everybody mixes up the kings sometimes.

That's what the LORD says: “Behold, I am about to deliver this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will burn it down.” (Jeremiah 34:2) It's a hard line to open with. The LORD says plainly what is coming. That's why the rest of the chapter matters.

A conqueror might do that, but the LORD doesn't say it here. He says the king of Babylon will take this city and burn it down (Jeremiah 34:2). Nothing about moving in or setting up shop. The word here is fire.

I wish it said that, friend, but it says the opposite. The LORD is about to deliver the city into the king of Babylon's hand, and “he will burn it down.” (Jeremiah 34:2) Untouched isn't in this message. I think this part of the chapter is heavy, and it's okay to say so.

True. The LORD tells Zedekiah, “And you yourself will not escape his grasp, but will surely be captured and delivered into his hand.” (Jeremiah 34:3) The king can't slip out a back door. The word is surely, and that's a firm word.

The text says the opposite. The LORD tells Zedekiah that he “will not escape his grasp, but will surely be captured and delivered into his hand.” (Jeremiah 34:3) Zedekiah has no escape plan that works. Even a king gets no sneaking out of this one.

Babylon it is. The LORD says to Zedekiah, “…you will go to Babylon.” (Jeremiah 34:3) He's captured, he meets the king of Babylon, and then he goes to the king's own country. That's a long trip for a man who started the day in Jerusalem.

Egypt does show up in this chapter, but as the land the LORD brought Israel's forefathers out of, the house of slavery (Jeremiah 34:13). It isn't where Zedekiah is headed. The LORD says plainly that Zedekiah will go to Babylon (Jeremiah 34:3). Wrong direction on the map, friend.

Nineveh is a city Jonah was sent to (Jonah 1:2), and it doesn't come up in this passage. Here the LORD tells Zedekiah, “…you will go to Babylon.” (Jeremiah 34:3) Babylon is the king's own land. Different city, different story.

Peace. The LORD says, “You will not die by the sword; you will die in peace.” (Jeremiah 34:4-5) That comes right after the hard news about capture and Babylon. It's a gentle line in a rough message, and it ends with the LORD saying He Himself has spoken it.
Poverty isn't in the message. The LORD says Zedekiah will not die by the sword and “you will die in peace.” (Jeremiah 34:4-5) The word is peace. Nothing about being poor.

With capture and Babylon in the picture, disgrace is an easy guess. But the LORD says, “You will not die by the sword; you will die in peace.” (Jeremiah 34:4-5) The word for how he dies is peace, not disgrace.

explanations.answer: Burn spices and lament for him
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “As spices were burned for your fathers, the former kings who preceded you, so people will burn spices for you and lament…” (Jeremiah 34:5) Zedekiah gets the same honor the earlier kings got. Burning spices is the kind of thing that fills a whole room. And the people grieve out loud.

explanations.answer: Carve his name on a great tomb
explanations.explanation: A tomb with his name on it sounds fancy, but the text doesn't say that. The LORD says people will burn spices for Zedekiah, as they did for the kings before him, and lament (Jeremiah 34:5). That's the honor He names. I've carved plenty of names, but only the Millers carved mine.

Songs about victories aren't mentioned. The LORD says, “…people will burn spices for you and lament, ‘Alas, O master!’” (Jeremiah 34:5) So it's burning spices and grieving, the same as for the kings before him. It's a quiet honor, not a parade.

I get why plenty sounds right when a whole kingdom is standing, but the text says the opposite. Babylon's army is fighting against Jerusalem and the remaining cities of Judah, including Lachish and Azekah. “For these were the only fortified cities remaining in Judah.” (Jeremiah 34:7) Two is not plenty.

False. The text says Babylon's army is fighting against Lachish and Azekah, and “these were the only fortified cities remaining in Judah.” (Jeremiah 34:7) Only two strongholds are left standing. That's about as close to empty as a cookie jar at midnight.

True. The word from the LORD is “…that each man should free his Hebrew slaves, both male and female, and no one should hold his fellow Jew in bondage.” (Jeremiah 34:9) Men and women both. Nobody gets left off the list.

The text says it differently. The word to Jeremiah was that each man should free his Hebrew slaves, both male and female, and no one should hold his fellow Jew in bondage (Jeremiah 34:9). That covers every Hebrew slave, men and women. I'm glad you gave it a try, friend.

explanations.answer: Until the people change their minds
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. The people agreed and released them, “but later they changed their minds and took back the menservants and maidservants they had freed…” (Jeremiah 34:10-11) Freedom that lasts until somebody changes their mind isn't much of a lock. I once vowed to stop sampling dough, and that lasted about one batch.

explanations.answer: For the rest of their lives
explanations.explanation: I wish that were the ending, friend. The text says they obeyed and released them, “but later they changed their minds and took back the menservants and maidservants they had freed…” (Jeremiah 34:10-11) So it didn't last their whole lives. The people took them back.

The text doesn't tie their freedom to the war ending. It says they released them, “but later they changed their minds and took back the menservants and maidservants they had freed…” (Jeremiah 34:10-11) The people changed their minds, and the servants were forced back into slavery.

Seventh. The LORD says, “Every seventh year, each of you must free his Hebrew brother who has sold himself to you. He may serve you six years, but then you must let him go free.” (Jeremiah 34:14) Six years of service, then he goes free. The LORD said it plainly when He brought them out of Egypt.

The number isn't ten. The LORD says, “Every seventh year, each of you must free his Hebrew brother who has sold himself to you.” (Jeremiah 34:14) He may serve six years, then go free. It's a seven, friend.

Third is too soon. The LORD says, “Every seventh year, each of you must free his Hebrew brother…” and that he may serve six years before being let go (Jeremiah 34:14). The count is six years of service, and the seventh year is when he goes free.

I see why that sounds good, but it's the opposite. The LORD says, “But your fathers did not listen or incline their ear.” (Jeremiah 34:14) The forefathers heard the law and didn't keep it. That's the history the LORD is bringing up.

False. After giving the law about freeing a Hebrew brother in the seventh year, the LORD says, “But your fathers did not listen or incline their ear.” (Jeremiah 34:14) They didn't follow it. That makes the people's recent freedom proclamation stand out.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: The LORD says they made the covenant “…before Me in the house that bears My Name.” (Jeremiah 34:15) That's His house, with His Name on it. They made the promise right there, in front of Him.

explanations.answer: In the courtyard of the king
explanations.explanation: The text puts it somewhere else. The LORD says they made the covenant “…before Me in the house that bears My Name.” (Jeremiah 34:15) It happened before Him, not in a courtyard. Even a king's courtyard isn't the place named.

explanations.answer: At the gate of the city
explanations.explanation: A city gate is a classic place for business, but it isn't what the text says. The LORD says the covenant was made “…before Me in the house that bears My Name.” (Jeremiah 34:15) That's the place He names.

explanations.answer: Free to go wherever they wanted
explanations.explanation: The LORD says the servants were “…set at liberty to go wherever they wanted…” (Jeremiah 34:16) That's real freedom, with no strings. Then the people took them back and forced them to be slaves again. That makes the turnaround hit harder.

explanations.answer: Free to work only for the king
explanations.explanation: That would be freedom with a catch, and the text doesn't say it. The LORD says they were “…set at liberty to go wherever they wanted…” (Jeremiah 34:16) No boss attached. The people later forced them back into slavery.

explanations.answer: Free to stay only inside the city
explanations.explanation: Staying inside the city would be a short leash, and that's not what the text says. The servants were “…set at liberty to go wherever they wanted…” (Jeremiah 34:16) Wherever they wanted is a wide-open door.

explanations.answer: Freedom to fall by sword and plague and famine
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says, “So now I proclaim freedom for you, declares the LORD…” and then names it: “…freedom to fall by sword, by plague, and by famine!” (Jeremiah 34:17) The people wouldn't proclaim freedom for their brothers, so the LORD uses their own word back at them. This one is heavy, and I think it's okay to let it sit.

explanations.answer: Freedom to be sold as slaves in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt shows up in this chapter as the land the LORD brought their forefathers out of, the house of slavery (Jeremiah 34:13). But that isn't the freedom He proclaims. He says, “…freedom to fall by sword, by plague, and by famine!” (Jeremiah 34:17) It's a hard line.

explanations.answer: Freedom to wander in the wilderness
explanations.explanation: Wandering isn't what the LORD says. He proclaims “…freedom to fall by sword, by plague, and by famine!” (Jeremiah 34:17) He does it because they didn't proclaim freedom for their brothers and neighbors. It's a heavy line, and I think it should be.

explanations.answer: By passing between the pieces of a calf
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD speaks of “…the calf they cut in two in order to pass between its pieces.” (Jeremiah 34:18) It's how they sealed the covenant before Him. And the LORD says those who broke the covenant He will treat like that calf.

explanations.answer: By writing it down on a scroll
explanations.explanation: A scroll makes sense, but the text names something else. The LORD says the covenant was sealed with “…the calf they cut in two in order to pass between its pieces.” (Jeremiah 34:18) That's how they bound themselves.

explanations.answer: By setting up a pillar of stone
explanations.explanation: A pillar is a good guess, but it isn't in this passage. The LORD says they made the covenant by passing between the pieces of a calf that was cut in two (Jeremiah 34:18). That's the picture He gives.

The text names a lot more than priests. The LORD lists “The officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the court officials, the priests, and all the people of the land who passed between the pieces of the calf…” (Jeremiah 34:19) The priests were part of it, and so was everyone else on that list.

False. The LORD lists “The officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the court officials, the priests, and all the people of the land who passed between the pieces of the calf…” (Jeremiah 34:19) The priests are on the list, but so are the officials and all the people of the land. It was a crowd, not just one group.

True. The LORD says, “I will deliver into the hands of their enemies who seek their lives.” (Jeremiah 34:20) It covers the officials, the priests and all the people who passed between the pieces of the calf. This is a heavy part, and the LORD doesn't soften it.

The text says the opposite. The LORD says of those who passed between the pieces of the calf, “I will deliver into the hands of their enemies who seek their lives.” (Jeremiah 34:20) He doesn't hold back from saying it. It's one of the heavier lines in the chapter.

explanations.answer: Bring them back to this city
explanations.explanation: Right. The LORD says, “Behold, I am going to give the command, declares the LORD, and I will bring them back to this city.” (Jeremiah 34:22) The army that had withdrawn comes back, and the LORD says it will fight against the city. He is the One giving the command.

That would be a relief, but the LORD says something different. He says, “…I will bring them back to this city.” (Jeremiah 34:22) The army that had pulled away returns at His command. I wish I had a gentler way to say it, friend.

Egypt isn't where this army is headed in this passage. The LORD says, “…I will bring them back to this city.” (Jeremiah 34:22) The city is Jerusalem, and the army returns to it. That's what He says He'll do.

Desolation. The LORD says, “And I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant.” (Jeremiah 34:22) It's the last line of the chapter, and it's a heavy way to close. The cities stand empty.

Battlefield fits the fighting, but it isn't the word used. The LORD says, “…I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant.” (Jeremiah 34:22) Desolation means the cities are left empty. That's a heavier picture than a battle.

Prison isn't what the LORD says here. He says, “…I will make the cities of Judah a desolation, without inhabitant.” (Jeremiah 34:22) The cities end up empty, with no one living in them. That's what desolation means.
